newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Winds,legal action delay SAfrica oil rig departure.
newsitem.headline: Winds,legal action delay SAfrica oil rig departure.

text.p: Heavy winds and legal action on Tuesday prevented the Soekor-Energy Africa Ltd oil rig, which will drill South Africa's first offshore field, from leaving Simon's Town as scheduled to start sea trials.

The rig, the Orca, was "arrested" late on Monday by the sheriff's office because of a 31 million rand debt owed by the French contractor Schlumberger, which has been refurbishing the rig, to local sub-contractor Babcock Construction.
This meant that the Orca would not be able to leave the harbour until some way had been found to settle the debt.
But Soekor rig manager Andre van Niekerk said that strong winds, rather than the arrest, had prompted the delay of the sea trials until Thursday.
"At this stage our departure estimate is Thursday morning and the reason for that is purely that we have had heavy winds these last few days," Van Niekerk said.
"It has really been pumping there. We need to load some equipment back on the rig before we can leave.
He said the legal situation was being monitored but that neither Soekor nor Energy Africa were implicated.
"Schlumberger have told us that they have posted a bond for 31 million rand so that the dispute can be settled in time and the claim can be aginst the bond and not the rig," he said.

Babcock legal representative Graham Charnock told Reuters that there was no intention to delay the departure of the rig, but Babcock had applied for it to be attached so that it could recover the money due to it before the rig sailed.
After the sea trials, which will take about three days, the Orca will be towed to the Oribi oil field off Mossel Bay.

Oribi is expected to initially produce 20,000 barrels of oil a day, with this amount tapering off over three to six years. It will form the nucleus for the subsequent development of several other nearby oil discoveries, which would extend production life by a further six years.
Soekor and its 20 percent partner, Energy Africa, plan to pump the oil into a one million barrel shuttle tanker for shipment to one of South Africa's three coastal refineries in Cape Town or Durban.
